en: 1. Mūlayamaka 1.2 Exposition (Niddesa) 1.2.1.
Exposition of the Chapter on Roots (Mūlavāraniddesa)
1.2.1.1. The Fourfold Guide on the Wholesome (Kusalapada Nayacatukka) 1.2.1.1.1.

The Guide on Roots (Mūlanaya) Are all those states that are wholesome (kusala) roots of the wholesome? There are only three roots of the wholesome. All remaining wholesome states are not roots of the wholesome.
Or again, are all those things which are roots of the wholesome (kusalamūla) themselves wholesome (kusala)? Yes.
Are all those things which are wholesome rooted in the same root as the roots of the wholesome? Yes.
Or again, are all those things which are rooted in the same root as the roots of the wholesome themselves wholesome?

Matter produced by the wholesome has a single root with the wholesome root, but it is not itself wholesome. That which is wholesome has a single root with the wholesome root and is also itself wholesome.
As for whatever phenomena have a single root with the wholesome root, are they all mutually rooted with the wholesome root?

Those roots that arise together are both single-rooted with the wholesome roots and mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with the wholesome roots have a single root with the wholesome roots, but are not mutually rooted.
Or, those which have mutual roots by way of a wholesome root—are all those states wholesome?
Yes. 1.2.1.1.2. The Method of Root-Roots:
Whatever states are wholesome, are they all rooted in wholesome roots? Only three are rooted in wholesome roots. The remaining wholesome states are not rooted in wholesome roots.
Or, are all those things which have the roots of the wholesome as their roots themselves wholesome? Yes.
Are all those things which are wholesome rooted in the same root as the roots of the wholesome? Yes.
Or, are all those things which are rooted in the same root as the roots of the wholesome themselves wholesome?
Matter produced by the wholesome has a single root-root with the wholesome root, but it is not itself wholesome. The wholesome has a single root-root with the wholesome root and is also wholesome.
As for whatever phenomena have a single root-root with the wholesome root, are they all mutually root-roots with the wholesome root?

Those roots which arise together are both single root-roots and mutually root-roots. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with the wholesome root have a single root-root with the wholesome root, but are not mutually root-roots.
Or, whatever states have mutual roots by way of a wholesome root, are all those states wholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.1.3. The Method of Roots:
Whatever states are wholesome, are they all rooted in the wholesome? Yes.
Or again, are all those things which have wholesome roots (kusalamūlaka) themselves wholesome (kusala)?
Material form originating from the wholesome (kusalasamuṭṭhāna-rūpa) has wholesome roots but is not itself wholesome. That which is wholesome both has wholesome roots and is itself wholesome.
Are all those things which are wholesome rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots? Yes.
Or, whatever phenomena have the same root as a wholesome root—are they all wholesome?
Matter originated by the wholesome has the same root as a wholesome root, but it is not wholesome. That which is wholesome both has the same root as a wholesome root and is itself wholesome.
Are all those phenomena that have the same root as a wholesome root mutually rooted in one another with respect to that wholesome root?

Those roots that arise together are both rooted in one another and mutually rooted. As for the remaining phenomena co-nascent with wholesome roots, they are rooted in the wholesome root, but are not mutually rooted.
Are all those phenomena which are mutually rooted with the wholesome root wholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.1.4. The Method of Rooted-in-the-Root (Mūlamūlaka-naya)
Are all those states which are wholesome rooted in wholesome roots? Yes.
Or else, are all those states which are rooted in wholesome roots wholesome?
Matter originated by the wholesome is rooted in wholesome roots but is not wholesome; the wholesome [state] is both rooted in wholesome roots and is itself wholesome.
Are all those states which are wholesome rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots? Yes.
Or again, are all those states which are rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots wholesome?

Material form originating from the wholesome is rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots, yet it is not wholesome. A wholesome state is both rooted in the same root as the wholesome roots and is itself wholesome.
Are all those phenomena which share a single root with a wholesome root mutually rooted with that wholesome root?

Those wholesome roots that arise together are both rooted with a single root and mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-arising with the wholesome root are rooted with a single root by virtue of the wholesome root, but they are not mutually rooted.
Are all those phenomena which are mutually rooted with a wholesome root wholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.2. The Fourfold Guide to Unwholesome States (Akusalapada Nayacatukka) 1.2.1.2.1.
The Guide to Roots (Mūlanaya):
Are all those states that are unwholesome roots of the unwholesome?
There are only three unwholesome roots (*akusalamūla*). Are all remaining unwholesome phenomena (*dhamma*) not unwholesome roots?
Yes. Or, are all those phenomena which are unwholesome roots themselves unwholesome? Yes.
Are all those phenomena which are unwholesome rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots?

Rootless unwholesome [states] do not have the same root as the unwholesome roots. Wholesome-with-root unwholesome [states] have the same root as the unwholesome roots. Are all those states which have the same root as the unwholesome roots unwholesome?
Matter originated by the unwholesome has the same root as the unwholesome roots, but it is not unwholesome. Unwholesome [states] both have the same root as the unwholesome roots and are unwholesome.
Are all those phenomena that share a single root with the unwholesome roots mutually rooted with those unwholesome roots?

Those unwholesome roots that arise together are both single-rooted and mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-arising with the unwholesome roots are single-rooted with the unwholesome roots, but are not mutually rooted.
Conversely, are all those phenomena that are mutually rooted with the unwholesome roots unwholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.2.2. The Method of the Root of Roots (Mūlamūlanaya) Are all unwholesome states (akusaladhamma) rooted in the roots of the unwholesome (akusalamūlamūla)?
There are only three roots of the unwholesome. All remaining unwholesome states are not roots of the unwholesome.
Or again, are all those things which have unwholesome roots as their root unwholesome? Yes.
Are all those things which are unwholesome rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots?

That which is unwholesome without a cause (ahetuka) is not rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots; that which is unwholesome with a cause (sahetuka) is rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots.
Furthermore, are all those phenomena which share the same root as an unwholesome root themselves unwholesome?

Material form originating from the unwholesome shares the same root as an unwholesome root, yet it is not unwholesome. That which is unwholesome both shares the same root as an unwholesome root and is itself unwholesome.
Are all those phenomena that share the same root as an unwholesome root mutually rooted in one another by virtue of that unwholesome root?

Those roots that arise together are both rooted in a single root—the unwholesome roots—and mutually rooted in one another. The remaining phenomena co-arising with the unwholesome roots are rooted in a single root by way of the unwholesome roots, but they are not mutually rooted in one another.
Are all those phenomena which are mutually rooted in one another by way of the unwholesome roots necessarily unwholesome? Yes, they are.
1.2.1.2.3. The Method of Roots (Mūlakanaya)
Are all those states which are unwholesome rooted in the unwholesome?
That which is unwholesome without a root is not rooted in the unwholesome; that which is unwholesome with a root is rooted in the unwholesome.
Or, conversely, are all those states which are rooted in the unwholesome unwholesome states?
Matter originated by the unwholesome has its root in the unwholesome, yet it is not itself unwholesome. That which is unwholesome both has its root in the unwholesome and is itself unwholesome.
Are all those states that are unwholesome rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots?
Unwholesome states that are rootless do not have the same root as the unwholesome roots. Unwholesome states that are with roots have the same root as the unwholesome roots.
Furthermore, are all those phenomena that share the same root as an unwholesome root themselves unwholesome?

Material form originated by the unwholesome shares the same root as an unwholesome root, yet it is not unwholesome. That which is unwholesome both shares the same root as an unwholesome root and is itself unwholesome.
Are all those phenomena that share the same root as an unwholesome root mutually rooted in one another through that unwholesome root?

The roots that arise together are unwholesome roots that both share the same root and are mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-arising with unwholesome roots share the same root as the unwholesome roots, but they are not mutually rooted.
Are all those phenomena which are mutually rooted with the unwholesome roots unwholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.2.4. The Method of Root and Sub-root (Mūlamūlaka-naya)
Are all those states that are unwholesome rooted in unwholesome roots?
That which is rootless unwholesome is not rooted in unwholesome roots. That which is wholesome-with-root unwholesome is rooted in unwholesome roots.
Or conversely, are all those states that are rooted in unwholesome roots unwholesome states?

Matter originating from the unwholesome has its root in the unwholesome roots, yet it is not unwholesome. That which is unwholesome has both its root in the unwholesome roots and is itself unwholesome.
Are all those states that are unwholesome rooted in the same root as the unwholesome roots?

Unwholesome states that are rootless do not have their root in the same root as the unwholesome roots; unwholesome states that are with roots do have their root in the same root as the unwholesome roots.
Or, whatever phenomena have a single root-rooted basis with an unwholesome root, are they all unwholesome?

Material form originating from the unwholesome has a single root-rooted basis with an unwholesome root, yet it is not unwholesome. That which is unwholesome both has a single root-rooted basis with an unwholesome root and is itself unwholesome.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root-rooted basis with an unwholesome root mutually root-rooted with one another by way of an unwholesome root?

The roots that arise together are unwholesome roots that share a common root-base and also serve as mutual root-bases for one another. The remaining phenomena co-arising with the unwholesome roots share a common root-base with the unwholesome roots, but do not serve as mutual root-bases for one another.
Are all those phenomena which share a mutual root-base with the unwholesome roots unwholesome? Yes.
1.2.1.3. The Fourfold Guide-Line on the Indeterminate Section (Abyākatapada Nayacatukka)
1.2.1.3.1. Fundamental Method (Mūlanaya):
Are all those states that are indeterminate (abyākata) indeterminate roots (abyākatamūla)?
There are only three indeterminate roots. All remaining indeterminate states are not indeterminate roots.
Or again, are all those things which have indeterminate roots themselves indeterminate? Yes.
Are all those things which are indeterminate rooted in the same root as the indeterminate roots?
That which is indeterminate and rootless does not share the same root as the indeterminate roots; that which is indeterminate and with root shares the same root as the indeterminate roots.
Or, are all those phenomena which share the same root as an indeterminate root necessarily indeterminate? Yes.
Are all those phenomena which share the same root as an indeterminate root mutually rooted with that indeterminate root?

Those roots which arise together are both indeterminate roots that share the same root and are mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with an indeterminate root share the same root as the indeterminate root, but are not mutually rooted.
Or again, are all those phenomena which have mutual roots by way of indeterminate roots themselves indeterminate? Yes.
1.2.1.3.2. The Method of Root-Roots:
Are all those phenomena that are indeterminate rooted in indeterminate roots?
There are exactly three roots that are neutral (abyākata). The remaining neutral phenomena are not roots that are neutral.
Are all those phenomena which are roots that are neutral necessarily neutral phenomena? Yes.
Are all whatever neutral phenomena there may be rooted in the same root as the roots that are neutral?
That which is rootless and indeterminate does not have a single root-root with an indeterminate root. That which is with-root and indeterminate has a single root-root with an indeterminate root.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root-root with an indeterminate root themselves indeterminate? Yes.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root-root with an indeterminate root mutually root-roots with that indeterminate root?

Those roots that arise together are both roots with a single root and roots that are mutual roots for one another. The remaining indeterminate (abyākata) states co-arising with indeterminate roots have a single root with the indeterminate root, but they are not mutual roots for one another.
Are all those states which are mutual roots with the indeterminate root necessarily indeterminate? Yes.
1.2.1.3.3. The Method of Roots (Mūlakanaya)
Are all those states which are indeterminate rooted in the indeterminate?
That which is indeterminate and rootless is not rooted in the indeterminate; that which is indeterminate and with root is rooted in the indeterminate.
Or again, are all those states which are rooted in the indeterminate indeterminate states? Yes.
Are all those states that are indeterminate (abyākata) rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root?
That which is indeterminate and rootless is not rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root. That which is indeterminate and with root is rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root.
Or conversely, are all those states that are rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root necessarily indeterminate states? Yes.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root with an indeterminate root mutually rooted with that indeterminate root?

Those roots which arise together as indeterminate roots are both single-rooted and mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-arising with an indeterminate root are single-rooted with the indeterminate root, but are not mutually rooted.
Conversely, are all those phenomena that are mutually rooted with an indeterminate root indeterminate? Yes.
1.2.1.3.4. The Root-and-Root Method (Mūlamūlakanaya).
Are all those phenomena that are indeterminate (abyākata) rooted in an indeterminate root?
That which is indeterminate and rootless (ahetuka) is not rooted in an indeterminate root. That which is indeterminate and with root (sahetuka) is rooted in an indeterminate root.
Or again, those which have the indeterminate root as their root— are all those phenomena indeterminate? Yes.
Whatever phenomena are indeterminate, are they all rooted in the same root as the indeterminate root?
That which is indeterminate and rootless does not have the same root as the indeterminate root. That which is indeterminate and with root has the same root as the indeterminate root.
Or again, are all those phenomena which share the same root-root with an indeterminate root themselves indeterminate? Yes.
Are all those phenomena whatsoever that share the same root-root with an indeterminate root mutually root-roots with that indeterminate root?
Those roots which arise together—the indeterminate roots—are both those that share the same root-root and those that are mutually root-roots.
And: The remaining states that are co-nascent with indeterminate roots have a single root-root with the indeterminate root, but they do not have each other as root-roots.
Are all those states which have each other as root-roots with the indeterminate root necessarily indeterminate? Yes.
1.2.1.4. The Tetrad of Methods on the Category of Mental States (Nāmapada Nayacatukka)
1.2.1.4.1. Fundamental Method (Mūlanaya).
Are all those phenomena that are mental (nāma) roots of mind (nāmamūla)?
There are only nine roots of mind. All remaining mental phenomena are not roots of mind.
Or again, are all those things which have name as their root called "name" (nāma)? Yes.
Are all those things which are names rooted in the same root as the root of name?
That which is name without cause (ahetuka-nāma) is not rooted in the same root as the root of name; that which is name with cause (sahetuka-nāma) is rooted in the same root as the root of name.
Or, whatever phenomena have a single root by way of being rooted in mind (nāma), are they all mind?
Matter originated by mind has a single root by way of being rooted in mind, but it is not mind. Mind has a single root by way of being rooted in mind and is also mind.
Whatever phenomena have a single root by way of being rooted in mind, do they all have each other as their roots by way of being rooted in mind?

Those roots that arise together are roots of mind (nāmamūla) that have both a single root and mutual roots. As for the remaining states co-nascent with the roots of mind, they have a single root with the roots of mind, but do not have mutual roots.
Or, are all those states which have mutual roots with the roots of mind necessarily mind (nāma)? Yes.
1.2.1.4.2. The Method of Roots and Root-Roots (Mūlamūlanaya)
Are all those phenomena that are called "roots of the roots of mind" (nāmamūlamūla) indeed such roots of the roots of mind?
There are only nine roots of the roots of mind. All remaining mental phenomena are not roots of the roots of mind.
Or conversely, are all those phenomena that are roots of the roots of mind indeed mental phenomena? Yes.
Whatever states there are that are mental, are they all rooted in the same root as the mental root?
A mental state that is rootless does not have the same root as the mental root; a mental state that has a root does have the same root as the mental root.
Or conversely, whatever states have the same root as the mental root, are they all mental states?
Matter originated by mind has a single root-root with the root of mind, but it is not mind. Mind has a single root-root with the root of mind, and it is also mind.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root-root with the root of mind mutually root-roots with the root of mind?

Those roots that arise together are both single root-roots with the root of mind and mutually root-roots. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with the root of mind have a single root-root with the root of mind, but they are not mutually root-roots.
Or, are all those phenomena which have their mutual roots in the root of mind (*nāmamūla*) called "mind" (*nāma*)? Yes.
1.2.1.4.3. The Method of Roots (*Mūlakanaya*):
Are all those phenomena that are mind-rooted (*nāmamūlaka*) necessarily mind? Yes.
Is that which is called "rootless name" not rooted in name? That which is "name with root" is rooted in name.
Furthermore, are all those phenomena which are rooted in name "name"?
Material form originating from name is rooted in name, but it is not name. Name is both rooted in name and is itself name.
Are all those phenomena which are mental concomitants (nāma-dhammas) rooted in the same root as the mental concomitant-root?
A mental concomitant that is rootless is not rooted in the same root as the mental concomitant-root. A mental concomitant that is with root is rooted in the same root as the mental concomitant-root.
Or again, are all those phenomena which are rooted in the same root as the mental concomitant-root mental concomitants?
Matter originated by mind has a single root with the root of mind, but not with mind itself. Mind has a single root with the root of mind, and it is mind as well.
Are all those phenomena that have a single root with the root of mind mutually rooted with the root of mind?

Those roots which arise together are both single-rooted with the roots of mind and mutually rooted. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with the roots of mind are single-rooted with the roots of mind, but are not mutually rooted.
Or, are all those phenomena which are mutually rooted by way of the root of name "name"? Yes.
1.2.1.4.4. The Method of Root-of-Roots:
Are all those phenomena that are names "rooted by the root of name"?
Is that which is called "rootless name" not rooted in the root of name? Is that which is "with-root name" rooted in the root of name?
Furthermore, are all those phenomena (dhammā) which are rooted in the root of name "name"?
Matter produced by name is rooted in the root of name, but it is not name. Name is both rooted in the root of name and is itself name.
Are all those phenomena which are mental (nāma), all rooted in the same root as the mental root?
A rootless mental state is not rooted in the same root as the mental root. A mental state with a root is rooted in the same root as the mental root.
Or conversely, are all those phenomena which are rooted in the same root as the mental root, all such phenomena mental?
Matter originated by mind has the same root as the root of mind; it does not [have the same root] as mind itself. Mind has the same root as the root of mind, and it is also mind itself.
Are all those phenomena that have the same root as the root of mind mutually rooted with one another through the root of mind?

Those roots which arise together are both rooted with the same root as the root of mind and mutually rooted with one another. The remaining phenomena co-nascent with the roots of mind have the same root as the root of mind, but they are not mutually rooted with one another.
Or, whatever states have mutual root-roots by way of name-root, are all those states "mental"? Yes.
This is the exposition of the section on roots.
